content:
Two contradictory reports appeared yesterday about next year's iPhone, which is said to be the 20th anniversary iPhone and is claimed to embody Apple's years-long vision of 'a single piece of glass.'

We've seen plenty of conflicting reports, but yesterday's divergence was perhaps the starkest yet…

Where things stand

Former Apple design chief Jony Ive has frequently spoken about his long-term vision for the iPhone, hoping that it would eventually become 'a single piece of glass.' Even though Ive has left the company, it's widely believed Apple still holds this vision.

Although Apple generally doesn't make a big fuss about product anniversaries, the prevailing view is that they want to achieve this vision as closely as possible for the iPhone's 20th anniversary. This design quite likely includes embedding Face ID under the display, and possibly even hiding the front camera beneath the screen.

However, we've seen plenty of conflicting reports. While the initial assumption was that this would be a standalone model, similar to the iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, more recent reports have indicated that this design would instead appear on next year's iPhone Pro models.

In sequence, it should be the iPhone 19 Pro, but Apple may skip this name due to the anniversary, jumping straight to the iPhone 20.

Yesterday's contradictory reports

Yesterday was made even more confusing by an analyst claiming that Apple had abandoned plans for an all-glass iPhone next year.

However, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman immediately came out to refute this claim.

The more likely scenario

The key point is that Apple's vision for the iPhone is not a single, finite destination. Whatever Apple plans to release next year will only be one step—perhaps several steps—toward the sci-fi 'single piece of glass' vision.

The question isn't whether this goal can be achieved next year, but how far Apple will move toward this vision. But whether it's one step or several, this certainly won't be the final step in the evolution of iPhone design.

In fact, Gurman says Apple has already made compromises on its original expectations for next year's design.

The Jefferies analyst may have heard the same information, but being closer to the source, interpreted it as Apple having abandoned the plan entirely.

My personal expectation is that next year's design will be a major leap—comparable to the giant leap of the iPhone X—but with more developments to come in subsequent years. For me, the biggest question is whether the 2027 iPhone will have made enough progress for Apple to adopt some kind of special naming approach, whether it's labeled as a 20th anniversary edition iPhone (which I think is unlikely), given some other special name, or skipping a generation to be called the iPhone 20 outright.

What are your expectations? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
